a:r.a:t: About one minute. Click 1 explains a decode step. Click 2 covers initial wait. Click 3 covers streaming speed. Click 4 connects generation to memory traffic.

Use the two questions in the title to make performance concrete. Time to first token measures the delay from submitting a request until its first output token arrives. It includes queueing and prompt processing, and may include network delay or model loading. With a warm model, processing a long prompt often makes substantial use of compute. Tokens per second here means the generation rate experienced by one user after output begins. Aggregate TPS across many users measures server throughput and should be labeled separately. An ordinary autoregressive decode step processes the current token through the model's layers and reads previous keys and values during attention. The cache is stored state, not a second neural network. A dense model uses its dense layers; an

model activates selected experts rather than every expert. Ordinary inference does not update weights. The new token's attention state is appended to the cache. For one or a few simultaneous sequences, weight and cache traffic can make decode sensitive to memory bandwidth. Long context increases attention work and cache traffic. Compute, optimized kernels, batching, and offloading also affect speed. Capacity determines whether the workload can fit; a larger memory pool does not automatically deliver faster generation. Compare the same model file, prompt length, output length, runtime settings, and concurrency. No speed benchmark is claimed on this slide.
